In the resource allocation graph, find a process Pi that is **neither blocked nor an isolated node** (that is, find a directed edge connected to it, and the request quantity of the resource corresponding to that directed edge is less than or equal to the number of idle resources currently available in the system.
As shown in the figure below, R1 has no idle resources, and R2 has one idle resource.
If all edges connected to this process satisfy the above conditions, then this process can continue running until completion, and then release all resources it occupies).
Eliminate all its request edges and allocation edges, making it an isolated node. In the figure below, P1 is a process node that satisfies this condition, so all edges of P1 are eliminated.
2. The resources released by process Pi can wake up some processes that are blocked waiting for these resources, and the originally blocked processes may become unblocked processes.
In the figure below, P2 satisfies such a condition.
After performing a series of simplifications according to the method in 1, if **all edges in the graph can be eliminated**, then the graph is said to be completely reducible.
